text: People ask what I did before this. Bit of everything, really. Not much of it on purpose. I was on the ferry for a long time, that's the one people know about. [dryly] Or think they know about. Anyway. Record.

First proper job I had was in a warehouse, loading lorries for a supermarket, the night shift nobody wanted. I was good at it, actually. I could stack a pallet so it would survive anything. I left because the supervisor kept calling me Kevin. I told him three times. The fourth time I just walked out, still in the yellow vest. I think I still have it somewhere.
Officially I'm not allowed on the ferry pier any more. There's a letter about it. Very polite letter. I've read it a few times. [dryly] They spelled my name right, at least. Here's a record.
Gerrit came with the boat. That's what I tell people, anyway. You buy an old trawler, you get the rust, the smell, and a herring gull on the roof who acts like he's on the papers.

I went abroad once to pick peaches with my friend Ruud. Six weeks, that was the plan. Ruud got homesick after four days and went home, and he took my sleeping bag with him by mistake. Or not by mistake, I was never sure. I did the six weeks. On a camping mat, with two jumpers. He still says he posted it.
Why did I leave the ferry? There was a small misunderstanding about a rope. That's the short version. In the long version there is a coastguard. Here's a record.

I tried to ride a moped to the south once. Fifty cc. Got about two countries in and it just stopped, on a slip road, and wouldn't start again. I pushed it to a petrol station and sat there most of a day. In the end I sold it to the man behind the till for the train fare home. [sighs] It was a good moped. It just didn't want to go south.

I was best man at Ruud's wedding. Yes, that Ruud, the sleeping bag. I left the rings in the van, at the other end of town. One of the bridesmaids had a car, and she drove me there and back, fast, talking the whole way about her sister's dog. We missed the vows. [quietly] Ruud forgave me eventually. She took a lot longer, but in the end she moved in, so.

My friend Henk says there's still a photo of me in the harbour office. Behind the desk, next to the tide tables. Not a good photo. I'm told people point at it. One day I'll go and have a look. Not yet.

I broke my wrist on a bet once. A lad said I could not get down the hill behind the church in a shopping trolley. I could. The bottom of the hill was the problem. Six weeks in plaster, and he never paid, because he said the bet was about going down, and I did not really go down, I went sideways into a wall.

I drove deliveries for a bakery for a while, bread to cafés and to the hospital. The van always smelled amazing, which is terrible when you are hungry. I was allowed to eat the broken ones. There were more broken ones when I was driving than before. I'm not saying anything. I'm just saying the numbers went up.

After the bakery I got on the ferry, as a deckhand. Ropes, cars, the ramp, cleaning up after people who had the soup. Eleven years. Honestly, the best job I ever had. I knew that boat better than my own flat. Every sound she made. I could tell you which light on the car deck was flickering and why. [quietly] I still could.

I bought a car once from a man in a car park. Paid far too much, I knew it while I was paying. It ran fine for eleven days. Then the exhaust fell off on a roundabout, and I drove around it three times trying to decide if I should stop. She was in the passenger seat. She didn't say a word. She didn't need to.

I said Gerrit came with the boat. He didn't. He came in the third week, sat on the aerial and put the station into static. I threw him a fish to get him off. Biggest mistake I made out here, and I made a few. He's been on the payroll ever since.

Every month a letter comes to Henk's address with my name on it. Brown envelope. He puts them in a shoebox under his stairs and doesn't ask. I don't open them. I know what's in them, more or less. [sighs] It's a big shoebox now.

For a while I drove the van for a band. You won't know them. Nobody did, that was a bit the problem. Four lads, me driving, carrying the amps, selling T-shirts at the back. About forty concerts, and I think we made money at two of them. The drummer still owes me for a tyre. [chuckles] I let that one go. Mostly.
She would have liked this one. She always said I hum the bit before the chorus and never the chorus itself. I never noticed until she said it. Now I notice every time. Anyway.

I washed pans in a hotel kitchen for a year or so. Pans, mostly. Mountains of them. The chef threw one once. Not at me, near me. So I quit, very proud, walked out. Came back the next day because I forgot my coat, and somehow I stayed another three months. Nobody ever talked about it. Me neither, until now.

Eleven years on that ferry, and I watched the captain take her away from the pier thousands of times. Hands on the wheel, the little levers, the way he leaned. I never touched any of it. Not once. But I knew exactly how it was done. Or I thought I knew, and that is a different thing, it turns out.

I had a landlord once who would not fix the boiler. So I stopped paying the part of the rent that I thought was the boiler. Worked it out on a calculator and everything. He took me to court and I lost, quite badly. But the boiler got fixed the week after. So, you know. You win some.

I came out here with a plastic bag of records, and I played them until they went grey. Then one day the keeper rowed out from the lighthouse. Never met him before. He had a fruit crate full of records between his knees, sand in half the sleeves. He held it up, said, these need playing, and rowed back. [warmly] That was it. That was the whole conversation.

I looked after a dog for a month once, for the old man next door when he went into hospital. Big stupid thing called Boef. He bit me the first day, and slept on my feet every day after that. When the old man came home, Boef sat in my hallway and would not go. I had to carry him. [wistful] Heavy dog. I still look twice at dogs like that.

Jan the engineer retired, after thirty years down in the engine room. We had a party for him on board, at the pier, after the last crossing, with a record player connected to the tannoy and too much of everything. And Jan said he had never once been upstairs when she was actually moving. Thirty years. So I said... one round of the harbour. [sighs] I can still hear myself saying it.

I have been in one fight in my life. In the queue at a chip shop. A man pushed in, and I said so, and he did not like that. I was right, and about four seconds later I was on the floor. [deadpan] I would still say it. I would just stand a bit further back.

It went well for about ten minutes. Really. Away from the pier, beautiful, out past the harbour wall, Jan on the bridge with his mouth open, music everywhere on the boat. Then I turned back a bit too early and put her on the sandbank at the harbour mouth. Not hard. Very gently. Completely stuck.

Nine hours we sat on that sandbank, waiting for the tide. The coastguard came. A tug came. Half the town came to the harbour wall to watch, and the record player kept playing on the tannoy, because nobody could remember where we plugged it in. People brought flasks of coffee. Somebody was selling chips. They tell me it was very gezellig. I could not really enjoy it.

The captain came out on the tug. He climbed aboard, walked up to the bridge, looked at me, looked at Jan, looked at the sandbank. Then he sat down in his chair, and after a while he said, Kees, was it worth it? And I said the first ten minutes were. [flatly] I was sacked before we were off the sand.

My friend Henk did the nicest thing anybody ever did for me. When everything went wrong, I slept on his sofa for five months, and he never once asked when I was leaving. Not once. He did start hiding the biscuits around the third month. That's fair. I would have hidden them from me too.

She said to me, not long before, if you do one more stupid thing, Kees. Just one. She was very calm about it. And then I took a ferry for a little trip. [quietly] So I can't really argue. I don't. I have something of hers on the shelf here, a hairband, it was in the car. I should send it back, really. I will. When things are a bit more sorted.

Then the letters started. The tug, the coastguard, the harbour, a day of crossings, a fence I don't remember hitting. A number I had to read twice. I didn't have it, and I was not going to have it either. So I did what every grown man would do. I borrowed Henk's dinghy and went to look at boats.

I bought this boat from a man up the coast. Cheap, because she was lying on the mud for years. Halfway through shaking hands he looked at me again and said, you're the ferry bloke. He was the skipper on the tug that pulled us off. [amused] He took a bit more off the price. He said it was the best laugh he had in years.

I anchored her just outside the island's waters. I worked it out with a chart and a ruler, about four times. It's not that I'm hiding. Everybody knows where I am, you can see me from the pier. It's more that letters have a harder time getting out here. And the view is nice.
I still have Henk's dinghy, by the way. The one I borrowed to go and look at boats. He never asked for it back either. I keep meaning to row it over. He's a good man, Henk. Better than me, anyway.

That captain still runs the ferry. She goes past here on the hour and the half hour, same boat, they got all the sand out. Sometimes, at the end of a good record, he gives a little toot on the horn. Could be hello. Could be, turn it down. I don't ask.

People ask how long I'm staying out here. Until it's sorted, I say. The letters, the money, me, in general. Then I'll row in properly, tie up at the pier like a normal person, get a haircut, see a few people. [clears throat] Anyway. Not yet. Here's a record.

I'll tell you the honest part. I thought I would hate it out here. I thought it would be a kind of waiting room. And it turns out I like it. Nobody tells me when to start or what to play. One chair, Opa coughing down below, Gerrit, records all day. [warmly] I took a ferry for a little trip and ended up with my own radio station. I don't recommend the route. But here we are.

That's more or less everything. There is more, there is always more, but this is enough for now. If you were on the harbour wall that day with a flask, watching a ferry sit on a sandbank playing records... [dryly] sorry about the noise. I hope you got some chips.
